claims.text: Under simultaneous abrasive and corrosive exposure, resistance in high-entropy alloys is governed by dynamic formation of an ultrafine, passivated surface layer.
The proposed ultrafine surface layer is induced by mechanically driven grain refinement.
The starting alloy is a homogeneous, near-random solid solution without a pre-engineered surface microstructure.
A combined thermal and mechanical surface pre-treatment can induce a nanocrystalline surface structure.
The pre-treated nanocrystalline surface readily forms a stable passivating oxide film.
A refined nanocrystalline near-surface layer promotes rapid regeneration of the passive film.
Mechanical abrasion causes severe plastic deformation and consequent surface grain refinement.
Surface grain refinement increases mechanical strength or hardness.
A refined microstructure accelerates formation of a protective passive film.
A stable oxide or passive film can reduce wear by protecting or lubricating the surface.
A stable passive film can reduce electrochemical corrosion.
Alloys lacking dynamic surface adaptation are less able to resist wear and corrosion simultaneously.
The pre-treated alloy will have a lower wear rate than an untreated alloy of identical bulk composition.
The pre-treated alloy will have a lower corrosion current density than the untreated baseline.
The pre-treated alloy will exhibit a more stable open-circuit potential than the untreated baseline.
The untreated baseline does not develop the dynamic nanocrystalline passivated layer.
The mechanism should operate when mechanical energy is sufficient to induce surface grain refinement.
The benefit should not manifest in low-strain or non-abrasive environments with little surface alteration.
The magnitude of improvement depends on alloy composition, processing parameters, and test conditions.

contradictions.description: The mechanism and boundary state that sufficient abrasion dynamically induces surface grain refinement, but the baseline is assumed not to develop the dynamic nanocrystalline layer despite undergoing the same abrasive test. No reason is given why abrasion would refine only the pre-treated surface.

The hypothesis attributes formation of the governing ultrafine layer to abrasion during service, whereas the intervention creates the nanocrystalline layer before testing. The comparison therefore does not cleanly distinguish dynamic abrasion-induced refinement from the effect of an initially pre-engineered surface.
